rationale: The retrieved PDF is the first author's 2026 doctoral dissertation, in which Chapter 2 (pp. 52-86; PDF pp. 69-103) provides the complete full text of the cited PLOS Water article ('Water supply and infrastructure challenges in rural low-income arid and semi-arid lands (ASALs): A case study of Turkana, Kenya'). The study uses a mixed-methods design combining a stratified cross-sectional household survey (n = 475), key informant interviews, six gender-stratified focus group discussions, infrastructure audits, and microbial/physicochemical testing of 91 water points. Among governance and legal-institutional mechanisms, institutional_structure_coordination clearly dominates: the study diagnoses fragmented devolved water governance across national (LOWASCO), county, NGO, and local actors, highlighting overlapping mandates, unclear lines of authority, and ambiguous ownership/mandates over legacy infrastructure that disincentivize rehabilitation and skew spending toward new capital projects (with participation_assistance—weak community involvement and Water Resource Users Associations—analyzed as a secondary theme). All core empirical outcomes—seasonal fetching distance and collection time burden, borehole operational functionality/breakdowns, service reliability, and microbial/chemical potability (E. coli, coliforms, fluoride, TDS/salinity)—belong to effective_access.
